cards.front: Is a pull request a feature of Git itself?
cards.back: No, it belongs to hosting platforms like GitHub or GitLab, which store it outside your repository.

cards.front: Set aside your uncommitted changes, including new files Git does not track yet
Bring back your most recently set-aside changes but keep them in the stash list
In a pull request's diff, what is your branch compared against?
cards.back: The commit where your branch split off the target branch, so later changes on `main` don't appear.

cards.front: Move the current branch back one commit, keeping that commit's changes staged
Discard your unstaged edits to `app.py` by copying back the version from the staging area
Delete your most recent stash without bringing its changes back
What happens to an open pull request when you push new commits to its branch?
cards.back: It updates automatically to include them, so you don't open a new pull request.

cards.front: What makes the commit created by a regular pull request merge different from a normal commit?
cards.back: It has two parents: the tip of the target branch and the tip of your branch.merge commitmain tipparent 1your branch tipparent 2

cards.front: Move the current branch back one commit, unstaging that commit's changes but keeping them in your files
Why does a merge conflict happen?
cards.back: Both branches changed the same lines differently since their shared starting commit, so Git cannot choose which version wins.shared starting commityour branch: line 5 = Aother branch: line 5 = Bconflict on line 5

cards.front: Show every set of changes you have set aside, newest first
If two branches both edit `etl.py`, do you always get a merge conflict?
cards.back: No. Git combines changes to different parts of a file automatically; only edits to the same or neighbouring lines conflict.

cards.front: What does `git merge --abort` do during a conflict?
cards.back: It cancels the paused merge and puts your branch and files back to how they were before merging.

cards.front: Does Git check that you removed the conflict markers before letting you commit?
cards.back: No. `git add` marks the file resolved even if markers remain, so leftover markers can get committed.

cards.front: Undo the latest commit by adding a new commit that applies the opposite changes
Show the full line-by-line changes saved in your most recent stash
What does "Squash and merge" add to the target branch?
cards.back: One new commit holding all the branch's changes; the branch's individual commits don't appear there.

cards.front: In a conflicted file, what sits between `<<<<<<<` and `=======`, and between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`?
cards.back: The first part is your current branch's version; the second part is the incoming branch's version.
